name: Pedro Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. Could you tell me about an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Pedro Larsen, 58, and I take the early bus to a housing site where I help with framing, doors and odd repairs. I like seeing a wall come square, though I am still learning and the faster carpenters sometimes have to show me a joint twice. Rain days and the ache in my knees wear me down more than the timber does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the site I would say the software is handy for checking a cut list, but the timber still has to fit the wall. I use it every morning, and I would tell the crew not to mistake a neat answer for a measured opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the hype fading would be a relief, but my pay is already low and there are hardly any other site jobs nearby. I am 58 and still learning pieces of this trade; one missed week empties what little cash we keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the early bus to the housing site and check the AI cut list against my tape, as I do now. During the first year I would put aside twenty from each full-pay week if there is any left after rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel steadier about the tools and still tight in the chest when the foreman sends people home for rain. A quiet AI story does not pay the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say a missed week matters, what happens at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ana works a few hours cleaning offices, and her hours move around too. If my site loses a week, we pay the rent first and delay replacing the leaking kitchen tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner hear from you after a normal shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ana the frame went up square and I got through another day without a mistake. I left school early, so learning by watching and checking twice is how I have kept working.

say: I use **AI cut lists** as a check, but my tape decides what fits.
I would tell the crew **site work** still needs people on the tools.
think: I feel relieved if the **hype fades**, because I can keep learning at my pace.
My **thin savings** mean an ordinary lost week still threatens our rent.
do: Keep taking the **early bus** to the housing site through the first year.
Set aside **twenty** from each full-pay week when bills allow.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, yet tense about lost site hours.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story does not pay the electricity bill.
fieldNote: Pedro treats AI as a **second check** against measurements, and knows its polished output can be wrong.
His **rent worry** predates AI; unstable construction hours and his partner’s variable cleaning shifts leave little buffer.

steps.text: Keep taking the early bus to the housing site
Set aside twenty from each full-pay week when bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman that software can order boards and plan deliveries, but somebody must sort the warped ones on site. I would also say the younger workers should learn the new ordering system instead of laughing at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may need fewer people and the building crews may get tighter targets once plans arrive instantly. My hands are slower than some, and low standing means I could be first off a short crew even before robots can frame a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the foreman to let me sit with the stores clerk one afternoon a week and learn the new ordering screen. In the first year of those changes, I would apply for the council maintenance openings if our crew loses hours, and skip the summer trip to our grown son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the screens and worried about who controls the hours. I like learning a tool, but I cannot learn away a cancelled Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you offer a maintenance employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can hang doors and patch damaged skirting, though I still ask a senior carpenter to check tricky joints. The council advertises maintenance jobs only now and then, so an application is a chance rather than a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound keen to learn, yet you are cutting a trip; why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to our son would take bus fares and three unpaid days, which we cannot gamble if the site shortens the crew. Curiosity costs less when I can practise on the store screen at work.

say: I would say **software ordering** helps, while warped boards still need a person on site.
I would urge younger workers to learn the **new system** before it changes crew routines.
think: I fear **tighter targets** could reduce my hours before any robot appears.
My **junior standing** makes me easier to drop when a crew is shortened.
do: Ask the **stores clerk** for weekly practice on the ordering screen.
Apply for **council maintenance** openings if site hours fall.
Skip the **summer trip** to our grown son if hours become uncertain.
feel: **Curious** about new screens and worried about cancelled shifts.
S1.quote: I like learning a tool, but I cannot learn away a cancelled Friday.
fieldNote: Pedro sees **office automation** reaching the building site through ordering and tighter schedules before physical robots arrive.
He is willing to learn, but his **application plan** depends on lost hours and scarce local maintenance openings.

steps.text: Practise the new ordering screen with the stores clerk weekly
Apply for council maintenance openings if site hours fall
Skip the summer trip to our grown son if hours become uncertain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that 2028 is too soon to pretend we have an answer, and the physical work has a little more time. I would ask the foreman to show us what the machines can actually do on a muddy site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 I would be 60; the plans and purchasing might be done by the new intelligence, and cheaper designs could mean fewer people paid to correct mistakes. By 2031 I would be 63, and if robots really handle site work, my junior job is in danger just when I need wages most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would photograph my finished door and repair work and put the pictures in a small job folder for maintenance applications. In 2029 I would keep taking paid site shifts and apply to the council maintenance team; if the robots take those tasks in 2031, I would ask the local training centre about building inspection classes I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be frightened at first, then start making lists because sitting still makes the fear worse. Three years of wages after the thinking systems arrive sounds useful until I remember how little we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Ana that I am making the work folder and still going to the site tomorrow. I would not promise her the council will hire me; she knows how few openings there are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection classes if the systems can think better than people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not sure inspection would survive the machines either, which is why I would ask about cost before enrolling. Someone may still have to visit a leaking house, but I cannot bank our rent on that guess.

say: I would tell the crew **2028 is soon**, and demand a real site demonstration.
I would say the **robot date** gives hands-on workers roughly three more years.
think: At **60**, cheaper AI plans could thin the crews even while people still handle timber.
At **63**, capable robots could take the site work that pays our rent.
do: Build a **repair portfolio** from photographed door and patching jobs now.
Apply for **council maintenance** work in 2029 while keeping paid site shifts.
Ask about **inspection classes** after robots arrive, enrolling only if affordable.
feel: **Frightened** by the speed, then occupied with lists.
S2.quote: Three years of wages after the thinking systems arrive sounds useful until I remember how little we have saved.
fieldNote: Pedro calculates the **2028 and 2031** dates against his need to work beyond age sixty.
His proposed inspection class is **conditional**; he openly doubts whether AI would leave that occupation secure.

steps.text: Photograph completed doors and repairs for a maintenance job application folder
Keep taking paid site shifts through the first year after 2028
Apply to the council maintenance team in 2029
Ask about building inspection classes and enroll only if affordable after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to stop guessing and start watching what actually happens to contracts. I would tell the crew to ask for paid practice on any new machines, not just a warning at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I might still be doing trim and repairs while the office plans itself. At 66 in 2034, robots that truly work with tools could take those shifts; I cannot assume retirement will cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the foreman to let me practise setting up the AI-assisted site measurement scanner and keep records of work I complete. In 2032 I would stay on paid repair shifts, but I would also submit applications to two building maintenance employers in the district; by 2034 I would ask about an affordable course in safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy, though five years lets me move one step at a time. The part that bothers me is not a clever machine; it is being 66 and still asking who has a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training centre about evening fees and grants, then enroll only if the cost left rent untouched. Ana and I do not have a pot big enough to buy a course on a hunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if neither maintenance firm answered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the site work for as long as the foreman offers it and ask the council for its vacancy list every month. I can make applications, but I cannot make an employer create a post.

say: I would tell the crew **five years** allows time to watch contracts.
I would ask for **paid practice** on equipment before the site changes.
think: At **63**, planning AI may change jobs while I still do repairs.
At **66**, capable robots could remove the shifts I still need.
do: Practise the **AI-assisted scanner** and record completed work now.
Apply to **two maintenance employers** in 2032 while keeping repair shifts.
Enroll in **safety checks** only if course fees leave rent secure.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to move through the warning years step by step.
S3.quote: I can make applications, but I cannot make an employer create a post.
fieldNote: Pedro uses the longer warning to seek **equipment practice** and document his work before making applications.
He refuses to assume a **pension** or that an inspection role will survive capable AI and robots.

steps.text: Practise using the AI-assisted site measurement scanner with the foreman
Apply to two district building maintenance employers in 2032
Keep taking paid repair shifts in 2032
Enroll in safety checks only if course fees leave rent secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives workers like me a chance to finish the years we can work, if the contracts hold. I would still want the site to train older hands on new equipment rather than leave us at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may be working fewer days by choice or because my knees demand it; I do not know which. At 71 in 2039, robots could do the remaining site tasks, and with almost no savings I cannot call that a comfortable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would try to add a little to our cash jar during full-pay months and talk with Ana about a lower-rent flat when our lease ends. In 2037 I would take any paid repair shifts I can manage, check the council vacancy board each month, and work out our real income before deciding whether to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more room to breathe, but not safe enough to celebrate. Ten years is a long time for a machine and a short time for a worker trying to build savings from the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another town for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana has regular cleaning clients here, and our grown children are nearby, so moving could cost us more than it earns. I would first look for a cheaper flat on the same bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make stopping work possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to see our rent and food covered without my wages for several months, not just hear that retirement is close. There is no pension figure in my hand that settles it.

say: I would say **ten years** could let me work longer if building contracts hold.
I would ask for **older workers** to get equipment training too.
think: At **68**, my knees and the contract may already have reduced my site days.
At **71**, robot work could end my shifts before we have enough savings.
do: Add money to the **cash jar** in full-pay months.
Discuss a **lower-rent flat** with Ana at lease renewal.
Keep taking manageable **repair shifts** in 2037 and check vacancies monthly.
feel: **Breathing room**, with persistent worry about retirement income.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time for a machine and a short time for a worker trying to build savings from the bottom.
fieldNote: Pedro sees the decade as time to earn, but **age and knees** may cut his working days before robots do.
His retirement decision rests on **actual rent coverage**, and he has no assured pension amount to cite.

steps.text: Add money to the household cash jar in full-pay months
Look for a lower-rent flat on the same bus route at lease renewal
Keep taking manageable paid repair shifts in 2037
Check the council vacancy board monthly in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because I would have almost no time to build savings before the office changes, then robots would follow in 2031. Paid practice with new site equipment and a clear list of affordable local courses would help more than a speech about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether there are enough jobs here for older beginners. There are not many, and a course only helps if somebody offers a paid shift afterward.

headlineQuote: You did not ask whether there are enough jobs here for older beginners.
portrait: Pedro is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker who left school early and learns by watching and checking twice.
He uses **AI daily**, yet trusts his tape and site experience over a polished cut list.
With **less than one month** saved, lost shifts threaten rent, even if AI mostly disappoints.
He keeps seeking **paid work** through each timeline and treats retraining as conditional on cost and vacancies.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** gives Pedro little time to build savings before thinking AI changes plans and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He asks for **paid equipment practice** and clear information on affordable local courses that lead to real shifts.
